content: Geraniol, also known as rhodinol, is classified as a monoterpenoid and an alcohol. It constitutes the primary component of oil-of-rose, palmarosa oil, and citronella oil (Java type). Additionally, it is present in smaller amounts in essential oils derived from geranium, lemon, and various other plants. Geraniol appears as a clear to pale-yellow oil, which is insoluble in water but dissolves readily in most common organic solvents. It possesses a distinct rose-like fragrance, making it a popular ingredient in the formulation of perfumes. This compound is also utilized in flavoring agents for a variety of fruits, including peach, raspberry, grapefruit, red apple, plum, lime, orange, lemon, watermelon, pineapple, and blueberry. Research has demonstrated that geraniol is an effective plant-based insect repellent. Interestingly, it is also produced by the scent glands of honeybees, where it serves to mark nectar-bearing flowers and guide bees to the entrances of their hives. In a 1994 report published by five leading cigarette manufacturers, geraniol was identified as one of the 599 additives used in cigarettes to enhance their flavor. Furthermore, geraniol and other flavor compounds naturally occur in well-aged tobacco. Under acidic conditions, geraniol undergoes a chemical transformation into the cyclic terpene alpha-terpineol. From a health and safety perspective, individuals with perfume allergies should avoid exposure to geraniol, as it may trigger allergic reactions.
